blackHole.title: Black holes
blackHole.description: Follow light around a black hole: lensing, orbiting matter, and the slow pace of time near the horizon.

orrery.title: Solar system
orrery.eyebrow: Orrery · The solar system in motion
orrery.description: How the solar system moves and how it was born: the planets where they are today, and how the young giants reshaped the paths of the small bodies, out to the Oort cloud.

deepField.title: Deep Field
deepField.eyebrow: Deep Field · As far as we can see
deepField.description: One zoom from the Sun past the nearest stars and galaxies to the oldest light we can see. The farther you look, the older the light.
deepField.edge: The edge of the observable universe

spectroscopy.title: Stellar Spectra
spectroscopy.description: Split starlight into its colours and read the dark lines: which atoms, how hot, how fast.

giants.title: Giants
giants.description: Climb from a city-sized neutron star past the largest stars to black-hole horizons, at true scale. Stop anywhere and open a star.

sun.title: The Sun
sun.description: One star, up close: cut it open, watch it in any light, fly over a sunspot and see a flare break loose.

voyage.title: Voyage
voyage.description: Fly a spacecraft from the Moon to the edge of the reachable universe, at true scale. Let the autopilot take you, or take the helm.
voyage.clocks: A ship clock and an Earth clock

about.title: Looking up, one sketch at a time.
about.lead: Horizon is my small collection of interactive simulations of space and gravity.

quote.text: I know that I am mortal, a creature of a day. But when I trace the crowded, circling spirals of the stars, my feet no longer touch the earth.

about.metadataDescription: Why I made Horizon, what it is for, and how to read its simulations.

course.label: The course
course.body: I started Horizon mostly as a supporting toolkit for <link>Astronomický kurz 2026/27</link> (1st year, in person), which I'm taking at Planetum.
course.next: I may add more simulations as the course goes on, if time allows.

disclaimer.label: A note on accuracy
disclaimer.body: I'm not a professional physicist or astronomer. I build the simulations with care and draw on published work, but they are meant mostly for exploration and the joy of discovery: illustrative aids, not an authoritative scientific source. Please take them with a grain of salt.
disclaimer.simplifiedBody: Models keep what matters for the idea and leave out the rest.
disclaimer.approximateBody: Values and scales are close, but not always exact.
disclaimer.performanceBody: Some physics is simplified further so the scenes run smoothly in a browser.
disclaimer.sources: For teaching, study, or anything that depends on exact values, please check primary sources.

source.label: Open source
source.body: Horizon is open source under the MIT licence: the code is on <link>GitHub</link>. Spotted a mistake? Issues and fixes are welcome.

imagery.label: Imagery
imagery.intro: Planet and moon maps, reprocessed for the orrery. Venus and Titan retain illustrative cloud and haze maps: radar or infrared surface maps would not show their visible appearance. Sedna has no resolved surface imagery; Halley’s partial flyby views do not provide a global spherical map. Uranus’s moons are painted from Voyager 2 views. These bodies remain explicitly illustrative. Maps are representative mosaics, not imagery for the selected timeline date.

tools.label: Tools
tools.intro: Used to build and check it.

items.sdoHmi: Sun: a representative mosaic of SDO/HMI observations from 1–22 May 2024. Reprojected and blended across one rotation; poorly observed poles fade to a quiet surface. The intensity map is displayed near white with limb darkening, not as a colour photograph. This is not live imagery or a single-date map. In the Sun lab it is the disc only at that epoch: as its clock runs, the spot groups are a model grown from it, drawn with the mosaic's own photographed groups.
items.opal: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune: Hubble maps from 2025, in true colour.
items.spacecraftModels: Voyager 1 and 2, Pioneer 10 and 11, New Horizons and Parker Solar Probe at their true size. Simplified and compressed, scaled to each dish's or heat shield's published width, and lit by the Sun in the scene.
items.blueMarble: Earth: October land and sea under a cloud layer.
items.jpl: Planet and moon orbits, Horizons positions and small-body data.
items.iau: Sizes, poles and rotation of every body.
items.nssdc: Radii, albedos, and the rings of Uranus and Neptune.
items.pds: Ring edges, gaps and opacities from Cassini and Voyager occultations.
items.gaia: Positions and motions of nearby stars, selected from Gaia DR3 and propagated with Horizon’s approximate motion model. ESA distributes Gaia data under CC BY-NC 3.0 IGO; commercial use requires ESA authorization.
items.simbad: Reference values for the bright and nearby stars.
items.gravity: Sgr A*'s mass and the Sun's distance from the Galactic Centre.
items.eht: The measured rings of M87* and Sgr A*.
items.codata: The gravitational constant, the electron's and proton's masses, the atomic mass constant, the classical electron radius and the Rydberg constant.
items.ciaaw: Atomic weights in the shared periodic table, from hydrogen to zinc.
items.nistAsd: Energy levels, ionization energies and transition probabilities for every atomic line in Stellar Spectra.
items.atlas9: Model photospheres of the stars in Stellar Spectra: temperature and pressure layer by layer.
items.barklem: Widths of metal lines broadened by collisions with hydrogen atoms in Stellar Spectra.
items.cie: The standard observer that turns spectra into the colours of stars, flames and the spectrum ribbon.
items.three: The WebGL rendering of every simulation.
items.meshoptimizer: Simplifying and compressing the spacecraft models.
items.solarProminences: Qualitative reference for the optional prominence model: plasma arches above the surface, seen as filaments against the disc. Horizon supplies the illustrative geometry, flowing plasma and simplified spring dynamics for growth, release and recoil. Pink/crimson colours approximate the visible-light appearance, with enhanced visibility. Positions and timing are authored, not observed events or a magnetic-field simulation.
items.moonMap: Moon: NASA's 2025 LRO/LROC colour mosaic, with laser-altimeter albedo filling the poles. Longitude is aligned to the globe; brightness is adapted for scene lighting. This is a processed visual map, not raw photometry.
items.ioMap: Io: Galileo and Voyager imagery. The source uses enhanced multispectral colour; we mute its saturation and adapt brightness without inventing surface features. The source interpolates the poles. This is not calibrated natural colour.
items.europaMap: Europa: the USGS Voyager/Galileo monochrome mosaic. The unobserved region south of 83°S uses a plain fill; colour is not inferred from brightness.
items.ganymedeMap: Ganymede: the USGS Voyager/Galileo multispectral mosaic, with muted colour and brightness adapted for scene lighting. Polar colour gaps use the source’s monochrome coverage; this is not calibrated natural colour.
items.callistoMap: Callisto: the USGS Voyager/Galileo monochrome mosaic. Missing coverage receives a plain fill rather than invented craters.
items.tritonMap: Triton: the USGS Voyager 2 synthetic-colour mosaic (orange, violet and ultraviolet filters), with muted saturation. The unobserved northern region uses a plain fill. Source grid lines were interpolated by USGS; this is not natural-colour photography.
items.phobosMap: Phobos: Philip Stooke's monochrome mosaic of Viking images with later Mars Express, Mars Global Surveyor and MRO views, on the DLR control network. Phobos is irregular; its map is drawn on a sphere.
items.deimosMap: Deimos: Philip Stooke's monochrome Viking mosaic with MRO HiRISE detail, from the NASA Planetary Data System. Deimos is irregular; its map is drawn on a sphere.
items.mimasMap: Mimas: DLR's monochrome Cassini atlas mosaic, with Herschel on the leading side.
items.enceladusMap: Enceladus: the USGS monochrome Cassini mosaic. Its albedo is near 1, so its brightness is held just below white to keep its terrain visible.
items.tethysMap: Tethys: the USGS monochrome Cassini mosaic, with Odysseus and Ithaca Chasma.
items.dioneMap: Dione: the USGS monochrome Cassini and Voyager mosaic, with the bright wispy fractures of its trailing side.
items.rheaMap: Rhea: the USGS monochrome Cassini and Voyager mosaic, with the rays of Inktomi.
items.iapetusMap: Iapetus: the USGS monochrome Cassini and Voyager mosaic. The mosaic evens out the dark leading hemisphere, Cassini Regio; we restore its contrast from the mosaic's own brightness, keeping the boundary where the data puts it.
items.ceresMap: Ceres: DLR's Dawn Framing Camera clear-filter mosaic from the 2015 survey orbit, as published by USGS. Brightness only, tinted Ceres's near-neutral grey; the south pole, unlit that October, is painted.
items.charonMap: Charon: the USGS New Horizons monochrome mosaic. The unobserved southern region uses a plain fill. No surface colour is inferred from the monochrome data.
items.feather: Original Feather icons used by Lucide, including navigation and interface controls.
items.ned: Galaxy and cluster positions and redshifts. This work uses NED, operated by Caltech under contract with NASA.
items.planck: Published cosmological parameters used for expansion, ages and distances. The drawn cosmic microwave background is illustrative; no Planck sky map is reproduced.
items.nearbyGalaxies: Local Group membership and nearby-galaxy properties, citing McConnachie (2012) and the October 2019 catalogue table.
items.gwosc: Published gravitational-wave event parameters, including GW150914 and GW231123. Values are selected and rounded for educational comparisons; Horizon does not replay detector strain data. Detailed citations and acknowledgements are in the scientific source record linked below.
items.naif: Reference radii, rotation poles and prime meridians. Moon orbits use JPL satellite elements and approximate fits to Horizons vectors, not a live SPICE calculation.
items.solarLimb: Red, green and blue coefficients evaluated from the SolarSoft darklimb_u and darklimb_v fits to Allen’s tables. Horizon applies an illustrative colour adjustment.
items.iauUnits: Astronomical unit, parsec, Julian year and nominal solar mass parameter and radius used across both simulations.
items.si: SI definitions underpinning units: the exact speed of light and the Planck, Boltzmann and elementary-charge constants.
items.helland: Adapted to GLSL and normalized RGB for the black-hole disk. This is an approximate display colour, not a calibrated spectrum.

Funding for the DPAC has been provided by national institutions, in particular the institutions participating in the Gaia Multilateral Agreement.

notes.changes: Maps were reprojected, resampled and filled where data is missing; <link>what changed in each map</link>.
notes.endorsement: Using NASA, ESA and USGS data does not imply their endorsement.
notes.papers: The <link>detailed scientific source record</link> lists catalogue sources, papers, model assumptions and unresolved measurement flags across both simulations. References remain in their published language.
notes.softwareNotices: Full copyright and licence texts for fonts and software, including bundled dependencies: <link>third-party notices</link>.
